newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president's son begs for mercy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president's son begs for mercy.

text.p: Dabbing his eyes with a handkerchief and occasionally sobbing, the son of South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Friday begged forgiveness as a "sinner" during a grilling by lawmakers over a loans scandal.
In a televised parliamentary inquisition, Kim Hyun-chul apologised to his father, but he denied taking bribes in the scandal that has rocked the nation.
The National Assembly is investigating his role in a loans-for-kickbacks affair surrounding Hanbo Steel Co, which collapsed in January under debts of $5.8 billion.
"I only beg for forgiveness from my father," he said, tears welling in his eyes. "I am a sinner to my father."
Kim Hyun-chul, 38, the president's second son, said he had been chiding himself for creating an "enormous social furore".
But he insisted: "I did not take money from Hanbo".
Opposition lawmakers accused Kim Hyun-chul of lying and said they had evidence. But they offered no proof.
Outside the National Assembly chamber, scores of people held a noisy protest to demand the arrest of Kim Hyun-chul.

The junior Kim, dubbed the "Crown Prince" by the media, countered charges by opposition politicians that he meddled in state affairs, including key appointments, and schemed with the help of the intelligence agencies.
"When my father asked me, I just recommended widely respected and outstanding people," he said.
"I'm praying for forgiveness, praying for my repentence and praying for hope. I deeply apologise to the people."
Ostentatious displays of remorse are not uncommon in South Korea, where a Confucian tradition requires that public figures be above suspicion. Unfilial behaviour is particularly reviled.
President Kim has also apologised over the loans scandal, taking "moral responsibility", and barred his son from public life. Neither Kim has ever admitted to any crime.

Kim Hyun-chul conceded that he recommended one of his associates for employment at the Blue House. The associate ended up working at the presidential mansion, although he was never formally on the pay roll.
He admitted meeting a top intelligence officer regularly but denied receiving intelligence agency reports.
"I believe I must be punished if I committed crime," Kim Hyun-chul said after being sworn in to give testimony. Asked if he violated laws, he said: "I don't think so."
Prosecutors have probed charges Kim Hyun-chul took a 200 billion won ($224 million) kickback from a business associate acting on behalf of Hanbo. He denied accepting any kickbacks.
Friday's hearing is the climax of a 45-day parliamentary probe into Hanbo that has tarnished credibility of a president who took office vowing to stamp out graft.
Political analysts said the son's testimony could further weaken the authority of the president, who has already become a lame duck in his last year of office.
Kim Hyun-chul conceded he might have appeared "pompous" by writing an autobiography, running a large office despite being jobless and discussing state affairs with his father.
"I am remorseful for what I have done," he said, revealing that he once considered running for parliament but dropped the idea when his father disagreed.
He denied rumours he kept unspent funds from his father's 1992 election campaign and had asked the founder of the Hanbo Group, Chung Tae-soo, to help launder the money.

Kim Hyun-chul, who played a key role in the campaign, brushed aside as groundless charges that he plotted to select a successor for his father, who is barred by the constitution from seeking re-election.
Chung is standing trial for corruption along with nine others, including the president's close associates, politicians and bankers in connection with Hanbo Steel's collapse.
